index_record.dataset_generation_caption:
The figure presents an overview of a method for dynamic scene representation and novel view synthesis using LiDAR data, structured into four main components labeled (a), (b), (c), and (d). The global layout is a 2x2 grid, with (a) and (b) on the left column and (c) and (d) on the right, connected by arrows indicating the flow of the pipeline. Each component is enclosed in a rounded rectangle with a distinct border color: (a) and (b) have a blue-gray border, while (c) and (d) have a greenish border, visually separating the representation and rendering stages from the output and fusion stages.

In (a) 'Dynamic Scene Representation', the scene is decomposed into a 'Background model' and 'Object model', both represented by Gaussian primitives. On the left, two boxes detail the properties of these primitives: 'Geometry' includes position (μ), opacity (α), rotation (R), and scale (S), illustrated with small blue ellipsoids; 'LiDAR Properties' shows spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients derived from directional radiance (r_dir), which are used to compute intensity (ζ) and raydrop (β). The background model is visualized as a dense, colorful point cloud with striped patterns, while the object model shows two cars rendered with smooth, gradient-colored surfaces. An arrow labeled 'T_local2world' points from the object model to the background, indicating coordinate transformation.

(b) 'Differentiable Ray Tracing Framework' illustrates the rendering process. A LiDAR sensor (a cylindrical icon) emits rays (black lines with direction arrows) through a semi-transparent scene composed of Gaussian primitives represented as translucent, faceted polyhedra. These rays intersect with the primitives, and the interactions are computed to simulate LiDAR responses. This module serves as the core rendering engine connecting the scene representation to the output views.

(c) 'Rendered Novel LiDAR View' displays three horizontal strips representing different LiDAR channels: 'Range' (top, colored by distance with blue-to-red gradient), 'Intensity' (middle, grayscale), and 'Raydrop' (bottom, binary black-and-white). These are the outputs generated by the ray tracing framework, simulating what a LiDAR sensor would capture from a new viewpoint.

(d) 'Novel View LiDAR Point Clouds' shows a 3D point cloud visualization, similar in style to the background model in (a), but with a denser, more structured distribution. An arrow labeled 'Fusion' points from (c) to (d), indicating that the rendered 2D views are fused and reprojected into 3D point clouds. This final step enables downstream applications such as 3D reconstruction or object detection.

The overall workflow proceeds from scene decomposition and parameterization in (a), through differentiable rendering in (b), to 2D view generation in (c), and finally to 3D point cloud reconstruction in (d), forming a closed-loop pipeline for dynamic scene understanding and novel view synthesis.
